claims.text: The protective coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure.
Spatially distributed secondary phases and precipitates create a heterogeneous microstructure architecture.
The heterogeneous architecture delays creep relative to a homogeneous architecture.
Secondary phases, precipitates, and heterogeneous interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The heterogeneous microstructure redistributes local stresses during sustained loading.
Precipitate–matrix boundaries and gradient phase distributions impede dislocation climb.
Well-spaced obstacles at heterogeneous interfaces reduce the creep deformation rate.
At identical sustained stress and temperature, the heterogeneous coating will have lower creep strain or creep rate than the homogeneous baseline.
Dislocation motion and plastic deformation occur more uniformly in the homogeneous baseline coating.
Significant phase transformations or precipitate coarsening can destabilize the heterogeneous architecture and reduce its effectiveness.
The proposed comparison uses coatings with identical overall alloy compositions but different homogeneous and heterogeneous microstructural states.
The comparison is conducted under identical sustained loads and elevated temperatures in the creep regime.
The general barrier-mediated creep-resistance mechanism is supported by microstructure-engineering principles.
The quantitative effect size and optimal secondary-phase distribution are uncertain.
Failure to observe a significantly lower creep rate in the heterogeneous state is designated as a falsifying result.
